hint: Inside which world is it computed?

choices.text: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
choices.why: It is computed assuming the null is true, so it cannot be the probability that it is.

choices.text: If the null were true, the chance of data at least this extreme
choices.why: Right. It measures how surprising the data would be in the world the null describes.

choices.text: The size of the effect, as a probability
choices.why: It mixes effect size with sample size and measures neither alone.

choices.text: The significance level chosen before the test
choices.why: That is α; the p-value is computed from the data and compared with it.

prompt: A one-sided test has p = 0.04, and the t distribution is symmetric. What is the two-sided p-value for the same statistic?
The routing test's one-sided p-value is 0.165. Which sentence states what it means?
hint: Read it as a frequency under the null.

choices.text: There is a 16.5% chance the new system does nothing
choices.why: That is the probability of the hypothesis, which a p-value is not.

choices.text: The new system saves 16.5% of delivery time
choices.why: A p-value is not an effect size.

choices.text: The result will be repeated in 83.5% of future trials
choices.why: A p-value says nothing so direct about replication.

choices.text: One sample in six would look this good by chance
choices.why: Right. Data like this is common when the routing changes nothing.

prompt: With α = 0.05, which p-value leads to rejecting the null hypothesis?
hint: Reject when p is below α.

choices.why: Right. Below α, so rejected.
Above 0.05: not rejected.
Just above 0.05: not rejected, though barely.
That is very ordinary data under the null.

prompt: Study A reports p = 0.049 and calls it significant; study B reports p = 0.051 and calls it not significant. How different is their evidence?

choices.text: Completely: one found an effect and the other did not
choices.why: The labels differ; the evidence is nearly identical.

choices.text: B's evidence is ten times weaker
choices.why: 0.051 is barely larger than 0.049.

choices.text: Hardly at all
choices.why: Right. A line at 0.05 makes two almost equal results sound opposite; report the exact p.

choices.text: It cannot be compared without the raw data
choices.why: The p-values themselves are directly comparable here.

prompt: The filling machine's test has p = 0.0009. Which conclusion is justified?
hint: Probability of the data, given the null.

choices.text: There is a 99.91% chance the machine is off target
choices.why: One minus p is not the probability of the alternative.

choices.text: The machine is badly off target, since p is tiny
choices.why: A tiny p says the effect is distinguishable from zero, not that it is big; the interval says 2.3 to 6.9 g.

choices.text: Such data would be rare if it were on target
choices.why: Right. That is exactly what the p-value measures.

choices.text: A second sample of 15 bags is sure to be significant too
choices.why: No single p-value guarantees replication.

prompt: Match each claim about p = 0.03 to what is wrong with it.

pairs.left: 'There is a 3% chance the null is true'
pairs.right: it gives the data's probability, not the hypothesis's
it mixes effect size with sample size
replication has its own, less flattering arithmetic

prompt: Most routing tweaks a supplier offers do nothing. A tweak's test gives p = 0.04. Why might it still probably do nothing?
hint: Out of all the tweaks with p below 0.05, how many are real?

choices.text: Useless tweaks' false alarms outnumber real wins
choices.why: Right. How likely a hypothesis is depends on what was plausible beforehand, which the p-value ignores.

choices.text: Because 0.04 is above 0.05
choices.why: 0.04 is below 0.05.

choices.text: Because p-values are computed incorrectly for tweaks
choices.why: The computation is fine; the interpretation is the issue.

choices.text: Because one test can never support an effect
choices.why: One test can support an effect; how much depends on the context.

prompt: Ten independent tests are run at α = 0.05 on true null hypotheses. What is the chance at least one is significant? Give two decimal places.
With a Bonferroni correction, what p-value must each of 10 tests reach for an overall α of 0.05?
hint: α divided by the number of tests.

prompt: An analyst tests delivery times by neighbourhood, by weekday and by hour, and reports only 'Barão Geraldo on Tuesdays, p = 0.02'. What is the problem?

choices.text: Tuesday is not a valid subgroup
choices.why: Any subgroup is valid to look at; hiding how many were looked at is the problem.

choices.text: p = 0.02 is too large to report
choices.why: Its size is not the issue.

choices.text: Barão Geraldo should be excluded as an outlier
choices.why: Nothing suggests that; the issue is selective reporting.

choices.text: One small p in many is just chance
choices.why: Right. Without saying how many subgroups were tested, the reader cannot judge the 0.02.

prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a mean runs from 36.62 to 41.18. What can you say about the two-sided test of μ = 40 at α = 0.05?
hint: Is the null value inside the interval?

choices.text: It rejects, since the interval is wide
choices.why: Width does not decide; whether 40 is inside does.

choices.text: It does not reject, since 40 is inside
choices.why: Right. A null value inside the 95% interval goes with p above 0.05.

choices.text: Nothing without the raw data
choices.why: The interval alone settles it.

choices.text: It rejects, since 40 is not the centre
choices.why: Values other than the centre can be perfectly consistent with the data.

prompt: Why is the routing interval, 36.62 to 41.18 minutes, more useful to a manager than 'p = 0.33'?

choices.text: Because intervals are easier to compute
choices.why: Both take the same arithmetic.

choices.text: It shows the trial cannot rule out a 3-minute gain, or none
choices.why: Right. The p-value only says 'not significant'; the interval says what the data still allows.

choices.text: Because the interval proves the system works
choices.why: It includes no change at all, so it proves nothing of the kind.

choices.text: Because the p-value is wrong for one-sided claims
choices.why: The p-value is fine; it just answers a narrower question.

prompt: Put the parts of an honest test report in the order this lesson recommends.
items: The estimate and its confidence interval
The test statistic, its degrees of freedom and the exact p
The hypotheses and level, and when they were set
An interpretation that claims no more than the interval allows

prompt: Which sentence reports a non-significant result honestly?

choices.text: The new system has no effect on delivery times (p = 0.16)
choices.why: Not rejecting is not proof of no effect.

choices.text: The new system is n.s.
choices.why: No estimate, no interval and no exact p: nothing a reader can use.

choices.text: The new system almost worked (p = 0.16)
choices.why: 'Almost worked' reads a weak result as a near success.

choices.text: Could not tell: from a 3-minute gain to a 1-minute loss
choices.why: Right. It states what the data allows in both directions.

prompt: A team keeps adding customers to an A/B test and checks the p-value every day, stopping the first day it falls below 0.05. What does that do?
hint: How many tests is that, really?

choices.text: It raises the false-alarm rate well above 5%
choices.why: Right. Every daily look is another test, and stopping at the first small p picks the chance dip.

choices.text: Nothing harmful; more data always helps
choices.why: More data helps; stopping when the result looks good is the problem.

choices.text: It makes the test more conservative
choices.why: It does the opposite: more chances to cross the line.

choices.text: It turns the test into a one-sided test
choices.why: The sidedness is unchanged; the stopping rule is the issue.
